body:
## Problem Nothing can react to a register changing. ## Solution This PR implements a new `RegisterChanged` event. The `autocmd-pattern` is the register name, and `v:event` contains the payload. ```vim " print a message when either register a or register b changes au RegisterChanged a,b echo v:event.regname .. ' is now ' .. string(v:event.regcontents) ``` ### Coverage Registers covered: - `"a`-`"z` (named) - `"0`-`"9` (numbered) - `""`, `"-`, `"*`, and `"+` (specials) - `"/` and `"=` (writable specials) - `":` and `".` (read-only) Registers **not** covered: - `"%` and `"#` (see below for details) ### Why? A plugin that mirrors or displays register contents would have to poll `getreg()` or use a `TextYankPost` autocommand. However, `TextYankPost` only covers yank, delete and change operators. It misses these cases: - `setreg()` - `:let @x =` - macro recording - numbered-register rotation - ShaDa load This feature was [initially proposed](https://github.com/vim/vim/issues/17843) upstream in Vim, but with little activity. ### Example Use Case: Live Register Display
Small example This cannot be done currently in Neovim. Note that there is **no `vim.schedule()`**. The event is deferred, so the handler already runs in a safe context. ```lua local shown = { 'a', 'b', '"' } local buf = vim.api.nvim_create_buf(false, true) vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('RegisterChanged', { pattern = shown, callback = function() local lines = {} for _, name in ipairs(shown) do lines[#lines + 1] = ('@%s = %s'):format(name, vim.inspect(vim.fn.getreg(name))) end vim.api.nvim_buf_set_lines(buf, 0, -1, true, lines) end, }) ```
## Design Decisions Details about the design of this PR.
The Pattern Is the Register Name Based on `OptionSet` and `MarkSet`. `au RegisterChanged a,b` subscribes to two registers. `` is the name. The name is always **lowercase**. Using `"Ayy` will append to `"a` and fire `RegisterChanged a` (because `A` is not actually a register). `*` is the one register name that collides with glob syntax, so `\*` is a working escape for the selection register.
Net-Change Semantics The event means **`@x` now reads differently**. It doesn't mean that a write happened. A write that doesn't change the value already there does not fire an event. A save+restore (below) also does not fire an event. ```vim let s:save = @a | let @a = 'x' | let @a = s:save " does not emit an event ``` The reference point to detect a change is the register's value _before the operation began_. This is a deliberate departure from `OptionSet`, which has no comparison at all. It is affordable performancewise because the write paths already free the old content, so the pending slot takes ownership rather than copying, and the comparison runs at drain time which is off the "hot path." The compared value is what the event reports (`regcontents` + `regtype`). **No two consecutive events for the same register will have identical `regcontents` and `regtype`.**
Deferred and Coalesced The `dev-new-event` doc asks for `aucmd_defer()`, and [#35366](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/35366) made that the default for new events. Deferral removes `textlock`, which lets callbacks write buffers directly. `aucmd_defer()` queues one item per call and deep-copies each payload, and `regcontents` _is_ the register. Registers are written in bursts, and an _appending_ burst grows the data being copied: running `:%normal! "Ayy` with a 10 000-line buffer appends to `@a` ten thousand times. The Nth deferred item would carry a copy of an N-line register. The queue then holds 1 + 2 + … + N lines before the first handler ever runs. For that 10 000-line buffer: | | Data queued before the first drain | | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------: | | This PR (coalesced) measured peak RSS (memory) | **+2.2 MB** over baseline | | One `aucmd_defer()` per write | **3 089.7 MB** | `:redir @a` over 10 000 writes reaches **6.59 GB**, which is clearly not good. So instead of enqueuing per write, a `pending[128]` table keyed by register is used. Keeping only the last payload is not sufficient on its own because snapshotting each write still copies 1 + 2 + … + N. So a pending slot stores the register _index_, and the drain resolves every live slot to a value before calling any callbacks. Nothing a callback does can change what a later event in the same drain reports. In other words, all active event subscriptions receive the same data per event instance. So we get **one all-in-one operation, one event per register that actually changed**. Intermediate values are never reported. > **Question**: this coalescing is implemented locally, in `register.c`. Does it > belong in `aucmd_defer()` generally? Any event that can fire in a burst has > the same exposure. For now it is kept local to avoid changing shared > machinery, but it could move if there's a better home.
`reason` Specifies the Mechanism There are 11 possible values (`yank`, `delete`, `shift`, `record`, `setreg`, `redir`, `shada`, `search`, `expr`, `cmdline`, and `insert`) for "the mechanism that wrote the register". It's called `reason` instead of `cause` because Neovim already uses this concept for `CompleteDone` and in the `v:event` glossary. This is documented as a listed set **with a growth clause**, meaning new values can be added later, and handlers must tolerate unrecognised values. Existing values will not be renamed or repurposed. This departs from `v:fcs_reason` and `CompleteDone`, which document closed lists. There is deliberately **no catch-all value** because `other` would let a future patch add a trigger site without classifying it.
This PR is Not Purely Additive It also changes `RecordingLeave`, under **BREAKING CHANGES** in `news.txt`. The register is now filled **before** `RecordingLeave` dispatches, so calling `getreg()` on the recorded register returns the new macro instead of the register's previous contents. - **Nothing diverges from Vim.** `RecordingEnter`/`RecordingLeave` are Nvim-only (`vim_diff.txt:350`). There is no Vim behaviour to match or break in either direction. - **The documented contract is preserved.** `reg_recording()` still specifies the register, and `reg_recorded()` is still only updated after the event — exactly as `autocmd.txt` specifies. `recording_spec.lua` asserts both from inside the handler and still passes. Only the register contents changed, which is why the fix moves the _write_, not the dispatch. - **The naive fix was never available.** Moving the dispatch to the end of `do_record()` breaks both assertions. - **The change is in code this PR already touches.** `do_record()` is where `reason = record` hooks. To be clear about scale, `v:event.regcontents` already contained the macro during `RecordingLeave` before this change. A handler was never unable to _see_ the macro, it just could not read it back out of the register. No upstream issue was filed for this. This was noticed while inventorying register write sites, and so is presented as an inconsistency found in passing, not a fix for a reported defect. In other words, it should be safe. **If you would rather have this split out, I can do that too.** The relevant files are - `src/nvim/register.c` (block move) - `test/functional/autocmd/recording_spec.lua` (new test) - `runtime/doc/autocmd.txt` (`RecordingLeave` paragraph) - `news.txt` `RegisterChanged` does not depend on this. The event is deferred, so it fires after `RecordingLeave` either way.
## Potential Objections Rationale about the design.
Why does this touch six subsystems? Registers have no single write funnel. `finish_write_reg` does not count. An analysis found **47 write sites**, and the special register writes do not live in `y_regs` at all: - `register.c` — the machinery, plus every `y_regs` site - `search.c` — `"/` is `spats[last_idx].pat`, including its save/restore wrappers - `insert.c` — `".` is `last_insert` - `ex_docmd.c` — `":` is `last_cmdline` - `eval/funcs.c` — one line, for the `setreg()` call that moves the unnamed pointer with no write - `autocmd.c` — **two lines**, adding the event to two existing lists Hooking `free_register` instead was considered and rejected. It is called on the clipboard _read_ path under `EXITFREE`, and the numbered rotation frees only `"9` while eight other registers change via struct assignment. The hooks belong at the write funnels. `clipboard.c` is untouched.
Why are ": and ". included? Because they turned out to be cheap and well-defined. `":` is `last_cmdline` with one write site; `".` is `last_insert` with two write sites. Their change points were already fixed. `":` is changed after execution and for typed commands only. `".` is changed at insert-leave rather than per keystroke.
Why are "% and "# excluded? Both of these registers are projections of window state, not stored content. `"%` is `curbuf->b_fname`. Covering it means hooking "`curbuf` changed" across **83 assignments in 28 files**, one being `aucmd_prepbuf()`, which would fire for switches not made by a user. Plus, everything it could report is already on `BufEnter`/`BufFilePost`. `"#` is worse: **11 sites outside `register.c`** write `w_alt_fnum`, and it is **window-local**, so `wincmd w` changes what `@#` reads with _zero_ writes anywhere. No set of trigger sites can cover this register. I argue that if you can't capture all the changes, it's better to not make it available rather than half-working and seemingly buggy. There is some amount of accepted asymmetry. `@#` is writable, so `:let @# = 'x'` is a register write with no event. Also, covering assignment only would have to use a fire-on-write method for `#` only (every other register uses the coalesced method).
Why no old register contents? vim/vim#17843 asked for "(and old?)" register contents. This was ruled out because it requires a deep copy before _every_ write, where the net-change design otherwise takes ownership of the freed value for free.
Why not use chrisbra's listener_expr_add()? The generic expression/variable listener counter-proposed in vim/vim#17843 is a different feature. It is a general watch mechanism over Vimscript values. This is an autocmd event over register state, subscribable by name, using the existing event surface that `OptionSet` and `MarkSet` already established. They are not substitutes, and this one needs no new concepts.
Why use v:event only, and no v: variable? `OptionSet` is `v:`-variable-only, so the question is fair. Nvim added `v:startreason`, `v:useractive` and a split `v:exitreason` this year. But they are a different channel. Each of these contains **global session state**, meaningful with no event in flight, while every `v:` variable that carries an **event payload** predates `v:event`. `reason` has no referent outside the event, so it is part of the payload. Cost was not the reason. The drain lives in `register.c` and a `v:` variable would have been about four lines. And a payload global has a real cost `v:event` does not: `OptionSet` must call `reset_v_option_vars()`. A pollable "last register change" readable outside the handler is out of scope. Nothing attributes it to a register, and coalescing can deliver several names in one tick. So a single global reports whichever drained last. `getreg()` already tells you the up-to-date contents.
Can a callback veto or transform the write? No, it is not possible. The event is deferred, so the register has already been written by the time the callback runs.
## Design Trade-Offs Discussion of downsides. Some may matter more than others.
1. **`points_to` can go stale.** The `""` event reports which register it aliases, but the pointer is not part of the compared value, so a move between two registers holding identical text is silent. If you cache this, then you drift. Must re-read `getreginfo('"').points_to`. But the alternative fires on moves that change nothing. 2. **A pointer flip between identical `"/` patterns is invisible**. `/foo` then `:s/foo/bar/` leaves both `spats[]` slots equal, so no event fires. 3. **Unset and empty are indistinguishable.** The payload always carries `regcontents`, so it cannot express "unset". `setreg('a','')` on a fresh register is silent. The event agrees with `getreg()` and disagrees with `getreginfo()`, which is what distinguishes unset and empty. A single empty _linewise_ line is correctly not conflated, however. 4. **`operator` and `visual` are filler unless `reason` is `yank` or `delete`.** The key set is uniform, so they are always present. `reason` tells you which fields are relevant. 5. **There is no `inclusive` key**, unlike `TextYankPost`. But its only documented use is as a modifier on `'[`/`']`, which a deferred event cannot keep in step with the payload. `TextPutPre`/`Post` already omits this for the same reason. 6. **An append is indistinguishable from a replace.** Coalescing makes an `append` flag incoherent — `"ayy` then `"Ayy` drains as one event whose last write was an append but whose net change is a full replace. 7. **`au RegisterChanged A` is a silent no-op on Linux.** Patterns match with `rm_ic = p_fic`, and `'fileignorecase'` defaults on for Windows/macOS only. This is the one piece of behaviour that varies by platform. No other event validates its pattern, so a warning would be new territory, not to mention wrong where it does match. 8. **A single `dd` can fire for registers the user never explicitly used**, because the numbered rotation is a real content change for `"2`-`"9`. On a fresh session, all nine slots stay empty and only `"1` fires. 9. **Nothing fires during `startup`**, including `-c`, `--cmd` and `-S`. This follows `OptionSet`'s precedent. Initial state can be read with `getreg()` upon `VimEnter`. `:rshada` afterwards _does_ fire events. 10. **A handler cannot observe its own register writes.** This is a livelock guard. A child-queue put pushes into the parent, which drains while non-empty, so without it `au RegisterChanged * call setreg('b','x')` would never terminate. This is `do_autocmd_textyankpost`'s existing policy, but enforced against the drain instead of the stack. 11. **`""` is emitted last**, not first as `:registers` shows it, because the alias must reflect the finished resolved state. 12. **`reason` specifies only the last write of a coalesced operation.** For instance, if a plugin that writes `"0` from a `TextYankPost` callback is loaded, a plain `yy` will report `reason: setreg`. 13. **`nvim_set_context()` fires with `reason: shada`**, because the context API uses ShaDa as its wire format. It's accurate, but may be surprising. 14. **A pattern-specific subscription still pays the full capture cost.** The write-path guard is `has_event()`, which is pattern-blind, so `au RegisterChanged a` captures and compares writes to _other_ registers before discovering that nothing matches. Below is some test data about this. | workload (2000 ops, zero events fired) | no subscriber | `au RegisterChanged a` | overhead | | -------------------------------------- | ------------: | ---------------------: | -------: | | 200 B appended to a 100 KB register | 134.13 ms | 477.53 ms | +256% | | `dd` (numbered shift) | 21.30 ms | 37.71 ms | +77% | | `setreg()` | 5.47 ms | 6.50 ms | +19% | | search (`"/`) | 130.51 ms | 137.02 ms | +5% | This should be considered acceptable because the absolute cost is 8–172 µs per operation against a 16 667 µs frame, bounded by one drain per user action, and the workloads that generate thousands of writes coalesce to **zero** measured overhead. So this does work and throws it away, but it doesn't cost much.
--- Claude was used to write most of this code, but human-facing descriptions and prose are painstakingly edited by me.

comment_data.body: adding a new, special-purpose structure is usually a red flag. there are already lots of "state holders", and the event system usually doesn't require a new one. maybe it's justified here, but it's the first thing i would try to iterate on and refine.
special-case functions instead of one central function `register_changed_capture` is a red flag
too much new, shared state. there must be a simpler way.
comment_data.diff_hunk:
@@ -998,6 +1057,491 @@ void free_register(yankreg_T *reg)
   *reg = (yankreg_T){ 0 };
 }
 
+// RegisterChanged
+//
+// The event reports net changes: it means "@x now reads differently", not "a
+// write happened". So a write is not an event on its own. Each write records
+// two things in a pending slot keyed by the register name - the value from
+// before the operation began, and the value it produced - and the slot is
+// drained at the next event-loop tick, where the two are compared and an event
+// is fired only if they differ.
+//
+// Deferring is what |dev-new-event| asks for, and it also makes a burst cheap:
+// further writes to a register that already has an undrained slot replace that
+// slot's payload instead of queueing a second event, so one all-in-one
+// operation produces one event per register it changed.
+
+/// Pending events, indexed by register name character.
+static RegChangedPending reg_pending[128] = { 0 };
+/// Whether a drain job is already on "deferred_events".
+static bool reg_pending_queued = false;
+/// Whether the drain job is running. Register writes made from a handler must
+/// not create new slots: a child-queue put extends the drain in progress, so a
+/// handler that writes a register would otherwise loop forever.
+static bool reg_draining = false;
